VS CODE EXTENSION DRIFT CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Did an extension you already trust just change what it does?

Paste a snapshot of your installed VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf, or VSCodium extensions and see exactly which ones changed their activation surface -- a new startup trigger, a new extension dependency, or a changed entry point -- since an earlier snapshot. Neither VS Code nor the marketplaces warn you when this happens, or when an extension you already have installed is later pulled for being malicious -- the mechanism behind the GlassWorm and Nx Console incidents.

Nothing is uploaded. The text you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device.

1. Paste your extension snapshot

2. What changed

Surface changed since the older snapshot

ExtensionVersionsRisk flags

Updated version only (no declared surface change)

ExtensionVersions

Newly installed

ExtensionVersion

No longer installed

ExtensionVersion

Activates unconditionally on every startup

Informational, not a finding on its own -- some extensions legitimately need this. Worth knowing which ones do.

ExtensionVersion

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file — and it can read your local extensions directory directly, which a browser cannot do:

node cli.mjs snapshot --out baseline.json     # scans your extensions dir, commit this once after review
# ...time passes; an extension auto-updates...
node cli.mjs snapshot --out current.json
node cli.mjs diff baseline.json current.json  # exit 1 only if something's surface changed
node cli.mjs diff baseline.json current.json --ignore ms-python.python
node cli.mjs check current.json               # live Marketplace lookup -- the only command that touches the network

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. snapshot and diff read only local files: no network call, ever. Only check talks to the network, from your machine, and only when you run it.

Real, dated incidents that used exactly this mechanism

CampaignMarketplaceSinceWhat happened

More: why VS Code doesn't warn you when an extension is delisted, and how to wire the CLI into CI. Comparing against a pre-install code scanner instead? See this checker vs. vsix-audit or this tool vs. VSCan.

Common questions

Why doesn't VS Code already warn me about this?

VS Code auto-updates extensions silently and has no mechanism to tell you an installed extension's activation surface changed, or that it was later pulled from the marketplace for being malicious. If you already have it installed when that happens, it keeps running with no notice — auto-update just quietly stops offering a newer version.

Is this a malware scanner?

No. It reports a structural difference between two snapshots of an extension's declared manifest fields (when it activates, what it depends on, its entry point), and a factual marketplace-resolution check. A flag means "read this one", not "this is malware" — it is not exhaustive and it is not a verdict.

Is my extension list uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses the snapshot you paste entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI's snapshot and diff commands read only local files — no network call, ever. Only the CLI's separate check command talks to the network, on your own machine, and only when you run it.

What do I paste in?

The output of node cli.mjs snapshot for the full picture, or the plain output of code --list-extensions --show-versions (Cursor and Windsurf have the same flag) for a quick id/version-only check.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It reports a structural difference between two snapshots of an extension's declared manifest fields, and whether an id currently resolves on the VS Code Marketplace — it is not a malware scanner, not a security audit, and not a guarantee that an unflagged extension is safe or a flagged one is dangerous. It does not replace reading the extension's source yourself or a qualified security review. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The text you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass over your dependency tree: npm Lifecycle Script Check diffs two snapshots of your package-lock.json for a newly gained install-time script — the same "paste two snapshots, get a deterministic diff" shape as this tool, for a different supply-chain surface.

Free and open source. If this saved you some digging, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-vscan.html.text:
← VS Code Extension Drift Check

This tool vs. VSCan

Different moments entirely: VSCan scans a named extension's code once, before you install it, to flag malware and excessive permissions. This tool diffs your already-installed extensions against an earlier snapshot to flag exactly what changed about them after you already trusted and installed them, or whether one you have was later pulled from the Marketplace.

What each tool is for

VSCan is a free, no-login static scanner. Its own site describes pasting in an extension's name or identifier and running a deep analysis of that extension's code, permissions, dependencies, and declared network activity, entirely before you install it — checking for malware and spyware, exploitable vulnerabilities, supply-chain risk inherited from dependencies, permission abuse, and privacy concerns. VSCan's own documentation is explicit that a scan is a starting point for review, not a guarantee, and that it can flag code it does not fully understand the intent of.

This tool does none of what VSCan does: it never downloads or inspects an extension's code, and it has no idea whether any single extension is malicious. It only compares two point-in-time snapshots of what you already have installed — by publisher, name, and version — to name exactly which ones changed their declared activation surface (a new startup trigger, a new dependency, a changed entry point) since an earlier snapshot, or a CLI-only live check of whether an installed extension's identifier still resolves on the VS Code Marketplace at all. That second question is exactly what let the GlassWorm and Nx Console incidents keep running on machines that had already installed a trusted-looking extension before it turned malicious or was pulled.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I'm about to install a new extension and want to know if its code looks malicious first.VSCan — that is exactly the pre-install job it is built for.
I want to know whether any of the extensions I already have installed changed their activation surface since I last checked.This tool — paste an older and a newer snapshot, get the diff.
I want to know whether an extension I've had installed for months was quietly pulled from the Marketplace.This tool's CLI check command — VSCan scans code, not Marketplace listing status over time.
I want a deep static analysis of one named extension's permissions, dependencies, and network calls.VSCan — this tool never reads an extension's code at all, only its declared manifest fields across two snapshots.
I want a one-time diff of exactly what changed between two lists of installed extensions, with no code scan involved.This tool — that is the whole job, and the only one it does.

A developer can reasonably use both, at different moments: VSCan before installing anything new, and this tool afterwards, on a schedule or in CI, to catch a silent change to what you already trust. This page does not evaluate VSCan's scan accuracy and makes no claim about it either way — it only describes VSCan's documented product shape and states what this tool does differently. A clean result from either one is not a security guarantee.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: the browser page and the CLI's snapshot/diff commands make no network calls at all, and the CLI's separate check command talks to the network only from your own machine, only when you run it.

Common questions

Does VSCan already catch an extension that changes after I've installed it?

Not in the way this tool does. VSCan's own site describes a one-shot static analysis: you give it an extension's identifier and it downloads and inspects that extension's code, permissions, dependencies, and declared network activity once, before you install it, to flag malware, spyware, exploitable vulnerabilities, supply-chain risk, and excessive permissions. That is a pre-install check on a single named extension. This tool does the opposite and narrower thing: it never scans an extension's code at all, and instead diffs two point-in-time snapshots of your own already-installed extension list, by publisher and version, to name exactly which ones changed their declared activation surface, or were later pulled from the Marketplace, after you already trusted and installed them.

Should I use this tool or VSCan?

They answer different questions and a developer can reasonably use both. VSCan answers "is this specific extension safe to install", with a deep, free, one-time code scan of that extension's bundle before it runs on your machine. This tool answers "did anything about my already-installed extensions change since I last checked, or did one of them get pulled from the Marketplace after the fact" — the exact gap that let the GlassWorm and Nx Console campaigns keep running on machines that had already installed a trusted-looking extension. Screen a new extension with VSCan before installing it, then use this tool afterwards to catch a silent change to what you already trust.

Is this page affiliated with VSCan?

No. This page is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by VSCan. It is named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, based on VSCan's own publicly documented product.

Open VS Code Extension Drift Check to diff your own extensions, or read why VS Code doesn't warn you when an extension is delisted for the full mechanism and how to wire the CLI into CI.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It reports a structural difference between two snapshots of an extension's declared manifest fields, and whether an id currently resolves on the VS Code Marketplace — it is not a malware scanner, not a security audit, and not a guarantee that an unflagged extension is safe or a flagged one is dangerous. It does not replace reading the extension's source yourself or a qualified security review. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Local-only privacy: nothing you paste on the linked tool is ever uploaded, and the browser page and the CLI's snapshot/diff commands make no network calls of their own. We count only anonymous feature events in localStorage, with an opt-out. This page makes no live comparison against VSCan — it is a static page describing publicly documented facts. License

Free and open source. If this saved you some digging, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-vsix-audit.html.text:
← VS Code Extension Drift Check

This checker vs. vsix-audit

Different moments: vsix-audit vets a named .vsix file for malware indicators before you install it. This tool diffs two point-in-time snapshots of extensions you already have installed and trust, to name exactly what changed or what quietly disappeared from the marketplace since your last check.

What each tool is for

vsix-audit is an open-source security scanner from Trail of Bits that you point at one named extension. It statically analyzes that .vsix file's code with AST-based pattern matching and YARA rules built from indicators of compromise drawn from known campaigns — GlassWorm and others among them — and reports findings as text, JSON, or SARIF, which fits it naturally into a CI gate on a specific package. It is a pre-install tool: the question it answers is whether a named extension looks safe to install in the first place, based on what its code actually contains.

This tool does none of that. It never downloads, unpacks, or statically analyzes an extension's code — it has no opinion at all about whether a given .vsix file is safe to install. What it does instead is read two snapshots of your own already-installed extension set (the output of node cli.mjs snapshot, or the plain output of code --list-extensions --show-versions) and diff them, naming exactly which extensions gained a new activation trigger, a new dependency, or a changed entry point since the older snapshot — plus a separate, CLI-only live check for whether an installed id still resolves on the VS Code Marketplace at all. It is a post-install, point-in-time tool, and the moment it targets is the one that mattered in both GlassWorm and the Nx Console compromise: extensions that were already trusted and running before anything changed.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is this specific extension safe to install, based on what its code actually does?vsix-audit — that is the pre-install code-scanning job it is built for.
Did an extension I already installed and trust change its activation surface since I last checked?This tool — paste two snapshots, get the diff, nothing installed or scanned.
Is an extension I already installed still on the marketplace, or was it quietly pulled?This tool's CLI-only check command — a live, factual resolution lookup, not a code scan.
I want YARA-rule and AST-based static analysis of an extension's actual code before I install it.vsix-audit — this tool never inspects extension code at all.
I want a CI gate on my whole team's already-installed extension set, not one named package.This tool — node cli.mjs diff baseline.json current.json exits non-zero on drift.

A team can reasonably run both: vsix-audit before adding a new extension to an allowlist, and this tool on a schedule against the whole already-installed set, to catch the drift or delisting that happens after an extension has already been trusted and approved. This page makes no claim about vsix-audit's detection accuracy either way — it only describes its documented shape and states what this tool does differently. Neither tool's clean result is a guarantee of safety.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the diff runs in your browser (or as a stdlib-only CLI script for snapshot/diff), and both keep working with the network off.

Common questions

Does vsix-audit already catch a drift in an extension I already installed?

Not in the way this tool does. vsix-audit, from Trail of Bits, is a scanner you point at one named .vsix file: it statically analyzes that file's code with AST-based pattern matching and YARA rules built from IOCs of known campaigns (GlassWorm and others), and reports text, JSON, or SARIF output, typically before you install the extension or as a CI gate on a specific package. It does not track your installed set over time. This tool does the opposite and narrower job: it never inspects an extension's code at all, and instead diffs two point-in-time snapshots of your own already-installed extensions to name exactly which ones changed their declared activation surface since an earlier snapshot, plus a separate live check for whether an installed id still resolves on the VS Code Marketplace.

Should I use this tool or vsix-audit?

They answer different questions, and a team can reasonably run both. vsix-audit answers "should I install this specific extension" by inspecting its code for malware indicators before it ever runs on your machine. This tool answers "did something I already installed and trust just change, or get pulled from the marketplace since I checked" — the question that matters after installation, which is also the mechanism behind the GlassWorm and Nx Console incidents: both involved extensions that were already trusted and installed before anything went wrong. Free, no account, no code sent anywhere either way.

Is this page affiliated with Trail of Bits?

No. This page is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Trail of Bits. vsix-audit is a project of Trail of Bits, named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, based on its own public GitHub repository and documentation.

Open VS Code Extension Drift Check to diff your own installed set, or read why VS Code doesn't warn you when an extension is delisted for the full mechanism and how to wire the CLI into CI.

It reports a structural difference between two snapshots of an extension's declared manifest fields, and whether an id currently resolves on the VS Code Marketplace — it is not a malware scanner, not a security audit, and not a guarantee that an unflagged extension is safe or a flagged one is dangerous. It does not replace reading the extension's source yourself or a qualified security review. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. why-vs-code-does-not-warn-you-when-an-ex.text:
← Back to VS Code Extension Drift Check

Why VS Code doesn't warn you when an extension is delisted

Delisting an extension from a marketplace stops it from being newly installed and stops it from being offered as an update. It does nothing to a copy already on a developer's disk: VS Code has no push mechanism that reaches back into an existing install to warn or remove it. If you installed the extension before it was pulled, it keeps running exactly as it did the day you installed it — auto-update just quietly stops finding anything newer to offer.

Two times this gap actually mattered

CampaignMarketplaceSinceWhat happened
GlassWormOpen VSX2026-01-31Self-propagating campaign that has abused at least 72 extensions, mimicking widely used linters, formatters, code runners, and AI-coding-assistant tools to reach developer machines.
Nx ConsoleVS Code Marketplace2026-05-18A trojanized build was live for roughly 18 minutes before takedown, distributing a credential stealer that harvested 1Password vaults, Claude Code configuration, and npm/GitHub/AWS tokens from anyone who updated during that window.

Sources: The Hacker News on GlassWorm, The Hacker News on the Nx Console breach. In both cases, developers who had already installed the compromised build before takedown had no in-editor signal that anything had changed.

What the two checks actually answer

The deterministic diff (snapshot + diff, no network) answers "did this extension's declared surface change since I last looked" — a new unconditional-startup trigger, a new extension dependency, or a changed entry point. It needs nothing but two snapshots you already have, and it works the moment an update lands, before anyone has reported anything.

The live check (check, the only command that touches the network) answers a different, narrower question: does this extension's id still resolve on the VS Code Marketplace right now. A "not found" result is the closest signal this tool can offer to "this may have been pulled" — but it is not proof. The same result appears for an extension that was never published to the Marketplace at all (installed instead from Open VSX, a `.vsix` sideload, or a private registry). Read it as a prompt to check by hand, not a verdict.

Wiring it into CI as a gate

Commit a reviewed baseline snapshot once, then compare against it on a schedule or before an image is rebuilt:

- name: Check installed extensions for a surface change
  run: |
    node ventures/vscode-extension-drift-check/cli.mjs snapshot --out /tmp/current.json --dir "$HOME/.vscode/extensions"
    node ventures/vscode-extension-drift-check/cli.mjs diff extension-baseline.json /tmp/current.json

The command exits non-zero only when an extension's surface changed since the baseline — a plain version bump, or a change on the side the browser page or a code --list-extensions-style snapshot cannot see, is reported but does not fail the build on its own. Accept a specific extension's change with --ignore id once you've reviewed it, the same way npm-lifecycle-script-check handles an accepted install script.

Common questions

If it's pulled from the marketplace, doesn't VS Code just remove it?

No. Delisting stops new installs and stops offering an update — it does not touch what is already on disk. An extension you installed before it was pulled keeps running exactly as before, with no dialog, no notification, and no automatic uninstall.

Does a surface-changed flag mean an extension is malicious?

No. The flags are a structural comparison against the incidents above (a broadened startup trigger, a new extension dependency, a changed entry point) — not a determination. A legitimate feature release can also add an activation event or a dependency. A flag means read this one; it is not a verdict.

Why check the Marketplace instead of scanning the extension's code?

Scanning bundled, often-minified JavaScript for malicious intent is a much harder, much less certain problem, and other free tools already attempt it. Checking whether an id still resolves needs no code analysis and no database: it is a direct factual question the Marketplace itself answers, and it is exactly the question a pulled-extension incident makes worth asking first.

No warranty. This page and the tool it documents report a structural difference between two snapshots of an extension's declared manifest fields, and whether an id currently resolves on the VS Code Marketplace. Nothing here is a malware scanner, a security audit, or a guarantee about any specific extension. Verify by reading the extension's source yourself before relying on it. Back to the tool.
